main_argument_chains.claim: managing the lowest lake means managing the highest one ahead of time
support_steps: the travel time from the highest lake to the lowest is about three months
the long program plans the releases over that horizon
the lowest lake's levels hold across the rain regimes while the highest lake's swing
main_argument_chains.decision_consequence: the authority is told to schedule the upstream dam with the downstream lake in mind

main_argument_chains.claim: two nested linear programs can serve the stakeholders without flooding
support_steps: each stakeholder is given an ideal curve and a weight
the long program keeps the levels inside the flood and drought bounds
the daily program is forced to end at the height the long one set
main_argument_chains.decision_consequence: the authority is offered both schedules, with the warning that the bounds sometimes make the program infeasible

warnings.warning: the flow penalty is weighted by one minus the sum of the stakeholder weights, so it is a residual rather than a named party's term and the objective depends on the weights not summing to one
Lake Erie's inflow is lagged by the travel time while the next equation gives Lake Ontario its inflow with no lag, so the delay is applied inconsistently down the chain

visualization_dispositions.analytical_purpose: show the lakes as a network and mark the two dams the model can move
show the two fitted lines the level balance rests on
show the long scheduler feeding the daily one
make the rain comparison visible, the achieved levels against the ideal
